title: You Don't Feel Like a Grown-Up? Neither Do I.
excerpt: Imposter syndrome doesn't always sound like fear. Sometimes it sounds like "I'm just not ready yet." Here's what the research actually says, and what helps.
body:
There's a specific feeling that shows up right when things are going well. You walk into a room where you technically belong, and some part of you is still checking the exits. That's not humility. That's imposter syndrome, and it doesn't wait for you to fail before it shows up. Sometimes it waits until you succeed.

### It's Not a Diagnosis, It's a Pattern

Imposter syndrome isn't in the DSM. It's not an official disorder, and I'm not interested in adding one more label to the pile. What researchers actually call it is the imposter phenomenon, and that framing matters, because a phenomenon is something your brain does, not something wrong with who you are.

Here's what it actually does: it takes a feeling and dresses it up like evidence. You feel unsure, so it tells you that you must be unqualified. You feel nervous, so it tells you that you don't belong. One mistake, and suddenly your brain is treating it like a federal investigation. I don't feel like a grown-up most days. I'm a father, and I've walked into jobs and interviews feeling like a kid wearing his dad's clothes, waiting to get caught. If that sounds familiar, you're not the only one.

### The Loop

Imposter syndrome isn't a single feeling. It's a cycle, and it runs in two halves.

The front half starts with an opportunity. You panic. Then you either overprepare until it's exhausting, or you procrastinate until the deadline is breathing on you. From the outside those look like opposites, one looks disciplined and one looks lazy, but they're often doing the same job: managing fear.

The back half starts after you succeed. Instead of pride, you feel relief. Then you explain it away: luck, timing, somebody being generous with you. The win doesn't build confidence. It just resets the clock, and the next opportunity feels more dangerous, because now people expect something from you.

### Five Ways It Shows Up

Researcher Dr. Valerie Young, through the Imposter Syndrome Institute, breaks imposter syndrome into five types. I've felt like all five of these at different points:

The **perfectionist** turns one mistake into the whole verdict. Ninety-nine things go right, and the brain zooms in on the one that didn't.

The **expert** believes not knowing everything means knowing nothing, which keeps you from applying for the job because of one bullet point you're not sure about.

The **natural genius** thinks that if something is hard, you must not be good at it, which punishes the exact effort every real skill requires.

The **soloist** believes needing help is the same as being exposed. Asking for support starts to feel like handing someone evidence against you.

The **superhuman** measures worth by how much you can carry before you break, and gets rewarded for it, which is exactly why it's so dangerous.

### Sometimes It's Not Just in Your Head

A lot of self-help content treats every feeling of not belonging as a personal confidence problem. Journal harder. Breathe deeper. Buy the mug that says believe. But that's not always true. Sometimes the room really is the problem, not just your read of it. If you're in a workplace, a family, or a community that keeps making you prove your right to be there, that's an environment issue, not a mindset issue. Both things can be true at once: your brain can be lying to you, and the room can also be genuinely off.

### What Actually Helps

The goal was never to stop feeling self-doubt. That's not realistic, especially when you're growing. The goal is to stop letting that voice drive.

Two things help me. First, keep evidence. Not vibes, not motivational quotes, actual evidence. A note in your phone with every compliment, every win, every hard thing you got through. Your brain is a terrible accountant. It remembers every mistake in high definition and files every win under "probably luck." You have to make the wins easier to find than the brain wants to make them.

Second, stop dismissing every win. If someone compliments you, let it land instead of handing it back. Luck plays a part in plenty of things, but luck didn't do the work, and it didn't carry the stress.

And if you want a gut check, use the friend test. If someone else had your exact experience, your effort, your results, would you call them unqualified? Probably not. You'd give them more grace than you give yourself, which means the problem was never the evidence. It was the judge.

### Maybe You're Not an Imposter

Maybe your life just grew faster than your self-image did. You have receipts now. You've survived things, learned things the hard way, and become someone people actually trust, even if part of you is still waiting for an adult to walk in and take over. The work isn't proving yourself from scratch every day. It's letting yourself catch up to what's already true.
